passages.title: Amazing Ants
passages.text:
Amazing Ants

What Are Ants?
Ants are insects that live in large groups called colonies. A colony can have millions of ants working together. Every ant has a job to do.

Types of Ants
There are three types of ants in a colony: the queen, the workers, and the males. The queen lays all the eggs. The workers find food and take care of the young. The males mate with the queen.

What Do Ants Eat?
Ants eat many different things. Some eat leaves, seeds, or other insects. Some even eat nectar from flowers.

Did You Know?
An ant can carry up to 50 times its own body weight!

questions.question: What is the purpose of the subheadings in this passage — such as "What Are Ants?" and "Types of Ants"?
options: To make the passage look longer
To help readers find information about each topic quickly
To tell the author's opinion about ants
To replace the need for a table of contents
questions.explanation: Subheadings divide a passage into sections and tell the reader what each section is about — they help readers find specific information quickly without reading everything.

questions.question: The words queen, workers, and males are in italic (slanted) print. Why did the author MOST LIKELY make those words italic?
options: Because they are the most interesting words
To show they are important vocabulary words
Because the author made a typing mistake
To show these words are made up
questions.explanation: Authors use italic or bold print to signal important vocabulary words — italics draw the reader's attention so they know these terms matter.

questions.question: Read the "Did You Know?" section. Why did the author MOST LIKELY include this section?
options: To summarize the main idea of the passage
To share a surprising fact that will interest readers
To explain what an ant colony is
To list the types of food ants eat
questions.explanation: "Did You Know?" boxes are used to highlight a surprising or fun fact that grabs readers' attention — the fact that ants can carry 50 times their weight is meant to impress and engage readers.

questions.question: A reader wants to find out what ants eat. Which subheading should the reader look under?
options: What Are Ants?
Types of Ants
What Do Ants Eat?
Did You Know?
questions.explanation: Subheadings tell the reader what each section is about. "What Do Ants Eat?" directly matches the information the reader is looking for.

questions.question: How does the bold title "Amazing Ants" help the reader?
options: It tells the reader the passage will be very long
It introduces the topic the whole passage is about
It explains what makes ants different from bees
It lists the main ideas of each section
questions.explanation: A title tells readers what the whole passage is about before they begin reading. "Amazing Ants" signals that the passage covers the topic of ants.

passages.title: Butterflies: Life Cycle
passages.text:
Butterflies go through four stages of life: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, and butterfly. First, a butterfly lays a tiny egg on a leaf. The egg hatches into a caterpillar, also called a larva. The caterpillar eats and grows. Then it wraps itself in a protective case called a chrysalis. Inside the chrysalis, it slowly changes. Finally, a fully grown butterfly breaks free.

Life Cycle of a Butterfly
[Graph: A circle diagram showing the four stages — Egg → Caterpillar → Chrysalis → Butterfly → back to Egg]

Caption: The butterfly life cycle repeats every season.

questions.question: What information does the circle diagram about the butterfly life cycle help the reader understand?
options: How long each stage of the butterfly's life lasts
That the life cycle repeats over and over in order
Which butterflies are most common in Texas
How big a butterfly gets when it is fully grown
questions.explanation: A circle (or cycle) diagram shows that a process repeats — the arrows going from one stage back to the egg show the life cycle continues again and again.

questions.question: Read the caption below the diagram: "The butterfly life cycle repeats every season." What does a caption do?
options: Replaces the diagram for readers who cannot see it
Explains or adds information about an image or diagram
Lists all the stages of the butterfly's life in order
Tells readers whether the diagram is accurate
questions.explanation: Captions appear below images or diagrams and explain what the image shows or add extra details — they help the reader understand why the visual is included.

questions.question: How does the diagram work WITH the passage to help the reader?
options: The diagram replaces all the information in the passage
The diagram shows the stages visually so readers can see the order clearly
The diagram gives information the passage does not include
The diagram is only for readers who cannot read the words
questions.explanation: Text features like diagrams support the written text — the passage explains each stage in words, while the diagram shows the stages visually so readers can understand the order at a glance.

questions.question: A student wants to quickly see what the four stages of the butterfly life cycle are. Which text feature would help MOST?
options: The caption below the diagram
The title of the passage
The circle diagram
The first sentence of the passage
questions.explanation: The circle diagram visually shows all four stages at once — it is the fastest way to see the four stages without reading through the whole passage.

passages.title: Animals of the Texas Prairie
passages.text:
Animals of the Texas Prairie

The Texas prairies are home to many interesting animals. Some are large and easy to spot. Others are small and hide in the grass.

Common Prairie Animals

[Table: Prairie Animal | What It Eats | Size]
Bison | Grass | Up to 2,000 lbs
Prairie dog | Seeds, roots | 2–3 lbs
Red-tailed hawk | Small animals | 2–4 lbs
Coyote | Meat, berries | 20–50 lbs

The bison was once nearly extinct but has made a comeback thanks to conservation efforts. Prairie dogs live in underground towns that can stretch for miles.

Glossary
conservation: the protection of animals and nature
extinct: when all animals of a kind have died out

questions.question: Look at the table "Common Prairie Animals." What does the table help the reader understand?
options: The history of how bison became endangered
The names, diets, and sizes of several prairie animals at a glance
Why prairie dogs build underground homes
How conservation programs work in Texas
questions.explanation: Tables organize information into rows and columns so readers can compare facts quickly — this table lets readers see each animal's diet and size without searching through paragraphs.

questions.question: A student does not know what the word "conservation" means. Which text feature would help MOST?
options: The table of prairie animals
The title of the passage
The glossary at the end of the passage
The bold subheading "Common Prairie Animals"
questions.explanation: A glossary defines difficult vocabulary words. The glossary at the end of this passage defines "conservation" — it is exactly the tool to use when a reader encounters an unfamiliar word.

questions.question: What are the MOST LIKELY reasons the author used bold subheadings like "Common Prairie Animals"? Select TWO correct answers.
options: To help readers skip directly to the section they need
To make the passage look colorful and decorative
To show the main topic of each section
To replace the glossary
To list all the animals found on Texas prairies
questions.explanation: Subheadings serve two purposes: they signal the topic of each section AND they help readers navigate the text by jumping to the section they need without reading everything.

questions.question: Based on the table, which animal weighs the MOST?
options: Prairie dog
Red-tailed hawk
Coyote
Bison
questions.explanation: The table shows bison weigh up to 2,000 lbs — far more than any other animal listed. Reading tables carefully lets you compare facts across rows.

questions.question: How does the glossary at the end of this passage help the reader?
options: It lists all the animals mentioned in the passage
It provides definitions for difficult words used in the passage
It summarizes the main idea of the passage
It shows maps of where prairie animals live
questions.explanation: A glossary is a mini-dictionary at the end of a text — it defines key vocabulary words like "conservation" and "extinct" so readers understand difficult terms without leaving the passage.

passages.title: How Plants Make Food
passages.text:
How Plants Make Food
By the Science Team

Plants make their own food through a process called photosynthesis. They need three things: sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide (a gas in the air).

[Diagram: A drawing of a plant with arrows showing sunlight hitting the leaves, water coming up from the roots, and carbon dioxide entering the leaves. An arrow labeled "oxygen" shows gas leaving the plant. A label at the center reads "Food (glucose) is made here."]

Caption: During photosynthesis, plants use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to make food. They release oxygen as a result.

Why It Matters
Photosynthesis is important for all living things. Plants release oxygen, which animals and humans need to breathe. Without photosynthesis, life on Earth could not exist.

questions.question: Look at the diagram of photosynthesis. What does the diagram help the reader understand that the words alone might not?
options: The definition of carbon dioxide
How sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide move INTO the plant and oxygen moves OUT
Why plants need to grow near water
How long photosynthesis takes to occur
questions.explanation: The diagram uses arrows to visually show the direction of each ingredient going in and oxygen going out — this movement is hard to picture from words alone, and the diagram makes it clear at a glance.

questions.question: Read the caption below the diagram. Which statement BEST describes what a caption does in an informational text?
options: It tells readers which part of the text is most important
It gives a brief explanation of what the image or diagram shows
It lists all the vocabulary words in the passage
It replaces the diagram when the reader cannot see it
questions.explanation: Captions explain or summarize what a diagram or image shows — they help readers who need additional context to understand the visual.

questions.question: The byline reads "By the Science Team." What does a byline tell a reader?
options: The main idea of the passage
When the passage was written
Who wrote or contributed to the text
Where the passage was published
questions.explanation: A byline identifies who wrote the text. Knowing the author helps readers evaluate the source — a "Science Team" suggests the information comes from experts.

questions.question: What are TWO ways the diagram and caption work together to help the reader understand photosynthesis? Select TWO correct answers.
options: The diagram shows the process visually with arrows
The diagram lists every type of plant on Earth
The caption explains what happens in words
The caption tells readers to memorize the diagram
Both replace the need to read the passage
questions.explanation: The diagram shows the process visually (arrows moving sunlight, water, carbon dioxide, and oxygen) while the caption explains in words what the diagram depicts — together they give readers two ways to understand the same idea.

passages.title: Who Jumps the Farthest?
passages.text:
Extreme Jumpers

Some animals are known for jumping incredible distances. Scientists measure how far different animals can jump to compare their abilities.

Who Jumps the Farthest?
[Bar Graph: X-axis = Animal (Frog, Grasshopper, Cougar, Froghopper, Kangaroo); Y-axis = Jump Distance in feet. Frog = 10 ft, Grasshopper = 3 ft, Cougar = 40 ft, Froghopper = 2.3 ft, Kangaroo = 25 ft]

Key Fact: Even though the froghopper is the smallest animal on the graph, it can jump over 100 times its own body length.

Scientists use data like this to understand how body structure helps animals survive in the wild.

questions.question: According to the bar graph "Who Jumps the Farthest?", which animal can jump the farthest distance?
options: Frog
Kangaroo
Cougar
Froghopper
questions.explanation: The bar graph shows the cougar's bar reaching 40 feet — the tallest bar on the graph — meaning the cougar can jump the farthest distance of all animals shown.

questions.question: The "Key Fact" box says the froghopper can jump over 100 times its own body length. Why is this fact surprising when you look at the bar graph?
options: Because the froghopper bar is the tallest on the graph
Because the froghopper jumps farther than the cougar
Because the froghopper has one of the SHORTEST bars, yet it jumps the most relative to its size
Because the bar graph does not include the froghopper
questions.explanation: The bar graph shows the froghopper jumps only 2.3 feet — one of the shortest bars. But the Key Fact reveals it jumps 100 times its own tiny body length. The contrast between absolute distance and relative distance is the surprising point.

questions.question: Why does the author include BOTH the bar graph AND the "Key Fact" box, instead of just one of them?
options: Because the bar graph is wrong and the Key Fact corrects it
Because the bar graph shows absolute distances while the Key Fact adds a different perspective — relative size
Because the Key Fact is required by law in science articles
Because both say the exact same thing in different ways
questions.explanation: The bar graph shows raw jump distances in feet (absolute). The Key Fact adds a new layer: how impressive a jump is relative to the animal's size. Together they give a more complete picture than either could alone.

questions.question: What does the Y-axis label "Jump Distance in feet" tell the reader?
options: The names of the animals being compared
The unit of measurement used to compare jump distances
The weight of each animal in the graph
Which animal is the author's favorite
questions.explanation: Axis labels on a bar graph tell you what is being measured and in what unit. "Jump Distance in feet" tells readers that all bars represent distance measured in feet, so they can accurately read and compare values.

questions.question: What are TWO things a reader can learn from the bar graph that are NOT directly stated in the passage text? Select TWO correct answers.
options: The exact jump distance of a kangaroo in feet
Why the cougar is a good hunter
The exact jump distance of a grasshopper in feet
How scientists measure jump distances
What froghoppers eat
questions.explanation: The passage text does not give specific numbers for kangaroo or grasshopper jump distances — those specific values (kangaroo = 25 ft, grasshopper = 3 ft) can only be found by reading the bar graph.
